questions.text: What key provisions should a contract establish to protect the architect's interests regarding abandonment and partial services?

options.text: The contract need not address abandonment; it is an uncommon occurrence, which is a risky assumption for any professional agreement
Milestone-based compensation percentages, payment for completed phases at abandonment, reimbursable expense coverage, change order procedures, and handoff documentation requirements
Only the total project fee; all other details are negotiated if abandonment occurs, which leaves the architect vulnerable to financial loss
The contract should guarantee that the client will not abandon the project, which is an unrealistic expectation in contract law

rationale.a: Underestimates risk; abandonment occurs frequently enough to warrant proactive contracting.
rationale.c: Leaves protection to post-abandonment negotiation; proactive contract language is essential.
rationale.d: Guarantees are impossible; contracts must specify compensation if abandonment occurs.
rationale.correct: Contracts should establish clear abandonment and partial services provisions: milestone compensation percentages, payment for completed phases, reimbursable expense coverage, change order handling, and documentation handoff requirements. This protects the architect and sets clear client expectations.
rationale.takeaway: Protective abandonment provisions include: SPP 202 percentages, payment-on-completion, expense coverage, change order procedures, and handoff documentation.

questions.text: When a project is abandoned, what happens to reimbursable expenses the architect advanced on the client's behalf?

options.text: The architect absorbs all reimbursable expenses as a loss, which can significantly impact their financial stability
Reimbursable expenses are due and payable regardless of project abandonment because they are actual costs incurred
Reimbursable expenses are forgiven if the project fails to proceed, as a gesture of goodwill towards the client
Only reimbursable expenses related to completed work are due; others are forgiven, depending on the terms of the contract

rationale.a: Incorrectly absorbs client-authorized costs; the client should reimburse.
rationale.c: Falsely forgives expenses; client authorization obligates reimbursement.
rationale.d: Incorrectly conditions reimbursement on work completion; all authorized expenses are reimbursable.
rationale.correct: Reimbursable expenses are legitimate project costs that the architect advanced on the client's behalf. The client should reimburse actual expenses regardless of project abandonment, as the costs were incurred with client authorization.
rationale.takeaway: Reimbursable expenses are due at abandonment even if the project doesn't proceed; they represent actual client-authorized costs.

questions.text: If a project is abandoned after the Design Development phase is complete, what percentage of the total SPP 202 fee has the architect earned?

options.text: 15% (Schematic Design only), which does not account for the Design Development phase
20% (Design Development only), which ignores the Schematic Design phase
35% (Schematic Design 15% + Design Development 20%)
85% (all phases except Construction Administration), which overstates the completed work

rationale.a: Calculates only Schematic Design; Design Development is also completed and compensated.
rationale.b: Calculates only Design Development; Schematic Design percentage is also earned.
rationale.d: Incorrectly includes Contract Documents (50%); Design Development completion is only 35%.
rationale.correct: The architect receives compensation for completed design phases. Abandonment after Design Development completion means Schematic Design (15%) + Design Development (20%) = 35% of the total fee.
rationale.takeaway: At abandonment, the architect receives fees based on completed phases: 15% (SchD) + 20% (DD) + 50% (CD) + 5% (Bid) + 10% (CA) based on where work stopped.

questions.text: If an architect is retained for Design Development services only (taking over from another architect who completed Schematic Design), what percentage of the SPP 202 total fee represents fair compensation?

options.text: 15% (Schematic Design rate)
20% (Design Development only rate)
35% (Assuming Schematic Design is automatically included)
100% (full fee regardless of which phases are included)

rationale.a: 15% is the allocation for the Schematic Design phase, not Design Development.
rationale.c: 35% would be correct if the architect were contracted for both Schematic Design and Design Development, but the question specifies Design Development services only.
rationale.d: 100% represents the full regular design services fee, not a partial service.
rationale.correct: If an architect is engaged strictly for the Design Development phase, compensation is based solely on the phase executed, which is 20% of the total fee under SPP 202.
rationale.takeaway: Design Development alone is 20% of the total architectural fee under standard SPP 202 phase breakdowns.

questions.text: How should a contract distinguish between project suspension (temporary halt) and project abandonment (permanent discontinuation)?

options.text: The contract need not distinguish; both are treated identically, which can lead to legal ambiguities
Clear language specifying that suspension is temporary with expected resumption, while abandonment is permanent, with differing compensation consequences
Suspension and abandonment are the same; no distinction is necessary, which is a common misconception
Only abandonment requires contract specification; suspension is assumed, which may not protect all parties involved

rationale.a: Identical treatment ignores different compensation implications.
rationale.c: Falsely suggests equivalence; suspension and abandonment have different implications.
rationale.d: Suspension requires specification too; both need clear contractual definition.
rationale.correct: Clear contract language distinguishing suspension (temporary with expected resumption) from abandonment (permanent discontinuation) protects both parties. Compensation consequences differ: suspension may involve retainer fees for maintained availability; abandonment triggers payment for completed work.
rationale.takeaway: Distinguish suspension (temporary, architect maintains readiness) from abandonment (permanent, architect paid for completed phases).

questions.text: What is partial services architecture engagement?

options.text: An incomplete engagement where the architect doesn't finish the contracted work, leading to potential disputes
A client engagement limited to specific phases (such as Design Development only, excluding Contract Documents and Construction Administration)
A project that is partially funded by the client, affecting the scope of services provided
An engagement where the architect only provides some of the required deliverables, based on client agreement

rationale.a: Confuses incomplete/abandoned engagement with deliberate partial services.
rationale.c: Describes funding issues, not partial services engagement structure.
rationale.d: Describes incomplete delivery; partial services is intentional limited scope.
rationale.correct: Partial services is a legitimate engagement where the client contracts for specific phases only. A client might retain an architect for Schematic Design and Design Development only, planning to engage another architect for subsequent phases.
rationale.takeaway: Partial services is intentional limited-scope engagement (SchD only, or SchD+DD) where the client will engage another architect for later phases.

questions.text: What is an abandoned project in architecture practice?

options.text: A project where the architect leaves the project before it is complete, often due to unresolved disputes or financial issues
A project where the client discontinues the project before completion
A project that continues but without client funding, leading to potential delays and incomplete work
A project that is redesigned by a different architect, usually after the original design fails to meet client expectations

rationale.a: Describes architect withdrawal; abandonment is client-initiated discontinuation.
rationale.c: Describes funding failure; abandonment is project discontinuation.
rationale.d: Describes design reassignment; abandonment is project discontinuation.
rationale.correct: An abandoned project is one where the client discontinues the project before completion. The client may abandon at various points: during Schematic Design, Design Development, after Contract Documents, or during construction.
rationale.takeaway: Abandonment is client-initiated project discontinuation at any phase; the architect retains fees earned for completed work.

questions.text: An architect completes Contract Documents and is not contracted to provide Construction Administration. The client manages construction independently. What is this engagement type and what fee applies?

options.text: Abandoned project; the architect receives 50% (Contract Documents only), reflecting the partial completion of services
Partial services (Design only); the architect receives 85% (Schematic through Contract Documents)
The architect must provide Construction Administration at no additional cost, as it is considered part of the standard service package
The contract is incomplete and must be renegotiated to clarify the scope and fee structure

rationale.a: Mischaracterizes as abandonment; this is intentional partial services.
rationale.c: Incorrectly obligates unpaid Construction Administration; contract limits scope.
rationale.d: Contract is complete as written; it deliberately excludes Construction Administration.
rationale.correct: This is partial services (Design only, without Construction Administration). The architect receives 85% of SPP 202 total fee for Schematic Design (15%) + Design Development (20%) + Contract Documents (50%).
rationale.takeaway: Design-only partial services = 85% of full fee (SchD 15% + DD 20% + CD 50%); Construction Administration 10% is intentionally excluded.

questions.text: A project is abandoned after Contract Documents completion. The architect has incurred 500,000 pesos in reimbursable expenses (consultant fees, site investigation, permits). The total design fee is 3 million pesos. What total amount should the client pay?

options.text: 2.55 million pesos (85% of 3 million design fee only; reimbursable expenses are forgiven, which is a common practice in some contractual agreements)
3.05 million pesos (85% of design fee = 2.55 million + reimbursable expenses = 0.5 million)
3 million pesos (full design fee; reimbursable expenses are separate and must be settled independently)
2.5 million pesos (50% of design fee as a compromise, which might be negotiated in cases of mutual agreement to terminate)

rationale.a: Includes design fees correctly (85%) but incorrectly forgives reimbursable expenses.
rationale.c: Incorrectly applies full fees when only 85% are earned at Contract Documents completion.
rationale.d: Underestimates phase percentage (85% earned, not 50%) and omits reimbursable expenses.
rationale.correct: At abandonment after Contract Documents, the architect receives 85% of design fee (Schematic 15% + Design Development 20% + Contract Documents 50%) = 2.55 million pesos. Additionally, reimbursable expenses (0.5 million) are due and payable. Total = 3.05 million pesos.
rationale.takeaway: At abandonment, architect receives: (applicable phase percentages × total fee) + all reimbursable expenses incurred.

questions.text: What documentation should an architect provide when transitioning a partial services engagement to another architect?

options.text: Only the final drawings; other documentation is the next architect's responsibility, unless otherwise agreed upon
Complete Design Development drawings, specifications, consultant coordination documentation, site investigation reports, cost estimates, program documentation, and design notes
No documentation is necessary; the next architect starts from scratch, allowing for a fresh perspective
Only a brief summary of design decisions; detailed documentation is confidential, protecting intellectual property

rationale.a: Inadequate; handoff requires comprehensive documentation beyond drawings.
rationale.c: Inefficient; comprehensive handoff prevents redesign of completed work.
rationale.d: Incorrectly treats design documentation as confidential; client owns the work product.
rationale.correct: Comprehensive handoff documentation facilitates continuity and allows the next architect to proceed efficiently. The first architect should provide complete Design Development deliverables, consultant information, and design rationale.
rationale.takeaway: Comprehensive handoff (drawings, specs, consultants, site data, cost estimates, program, design rationale) enables the next architect to proceed efficiently.
